data_source: UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (Anguita et al., 2013), CC BY 4.0

spotlight.explanation: Volunteer 9 was truly climbing stairs (up), but the network said 'walking' with 100% confidence. This window had a step rhythm of 1.86 steps per second (typical walking: 1.76; typical climbing stairs (up): 1.61); and an up-down bounce of 0.150 g (typical walking: 0.220 g; typical climbing stairs (up): 0.249 g); and a strongest jolt of 0.45 g (typical walking: 0.69 g; typical climbing stairs (up): 0.75 g). Those numbers look more like the predicted activity than the real one in the training data. An accelerometer can't feel height change directly, so walking and stairs can look alike. Things that might have helped: a barometer (air-pressure) reading that shows going up or down, longer windows so the model sees more steps, the gyroscope signals the dataset also includes, or more training volunteers with different walking styles.
